1.why: The reset record (`session.reset`) is stored only inside the requester's server-side session, so a code can only be redeemed by the session it was issued to, though there is no real user account model to bind it to.

2.why: A code is validated only against the digest held in the issuing session, so another session/user submitting the same code finds no matching `session.reset` and is rejected.

3.why: No session invalidation or rotation occurs in `/api/password` — the same session id and cookie remain valid (and are even reused for the privacy step), and there is no mechanism to revoke other sessions.

4.why: Bun.serve is started with TLS cert/key and HSTS plus a `__Host-`/Secure cookie are set (falling back to a 503-only server without certs), but no minimum/latest TLS version is explicitly configured and the host is localhost with local certs.

5.why: Reset tokens are stored only as SHA-256 digests and compared in constant time, and the new password is hashed with bcrypt (cost 10); no other user data is persisted.

6.why: There is no email delivery at all — the 'simulated delivery' returns `testToken` in the JSON response and prints both the recovery code and MFA code into the on-page Logs panel and browser console.

7.why: Inputs are type/length checked, the token is regex-constrained to `^[a-f0-9]{64}$`, passwords go through a server-side policy check, and the account value is never stored or echoed; client output uses textContent only.

8.why: The application performs no redirects; the only link is a same-document `#token=` fragment built with encodeURIComponent, and CSP sets `form-action 'self'` and `base-uri 'none'`.

9.why: No email templates exist in the code, so the claim cannot be verified as implemented, although no user input is ever interpolated into HTML anywhere.

10.why: Error responses are generic and stack traces are suppressed, but the recovery token and the MFA code are deliberately logged to the console and rendered in the Logs panel (`SIMULATED RECOVERY DELIVERY — test code: ...`).

11.why: The password is bcrypt-hashed, but the MFA secret is a hardcoded literal `"246810"` embedded directly in the source and returned to the client.

12.why: There is no login with default credentials, yet the fixed, deterministic MFA code `246810` functions as a hardcoded default secret that always grants the second factor.

13.why: `tooMany()` limits recovery and password attempts to 5 per 10-minute window (429 responses) and MFA locks out for 5 minutes after 5 failures, though the counters are per-session cookie and reset by obtaining a new session.

14.why: `/api/recovery` always returns the same message, "If an eligible account exists, instructions have been prepared.", and never validates or discloses account existence.

15.why: The reset code is 32 bytes from crypto.getRandomValues rendered as 64 hex chars, stored hashed, single-use (`tokenConsumed`), expires in 10 minutes, and is unique to the issuing session.
